Pilot Sample Size for Bounded Risk Point Estimation of a Normal Mean

Source: R/seq_br_norm_mean.R
seq_br_norm_mean_pilot.Rd

Returns the number of observations to collect before the stopping rule of seq_br_norm_mean is checked for the first time. That procedure is the purely sequential bounded risk point estimator of the mean of a normal population with unknown variance (Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009).

Usage

seq_br_norm_mean_pilot(A, k, w, m_0 = 10, gamma = 1)

Arguments

A

The loss constant: the loss from estimating the mean \(\mu\) by the sample mean is \(A\,|\bar{X}_n - \mu|^k\). A positive number; it sets the units in which the risk bound w is expressed (use A = 1 to bound the mean absolute or mean squared error itself).

k

The power in the loss: 1 for absolute error, 2 for squared error.

w

The risk bound: the largest expected loss that is acceptable. A positive number, in the units of A times the data's units to the power k.

m_0

The smallest pilot sample size allowed. A whole number of at least 2; default 10. A larger value reduces the amount by which the risk can exceed the bound when the bound is loose (see the Details of seq_br_norm_mean); it costs at most m_0 observations.

gamma

Positive constant that sets how fast the pilot grows as the bound tightens; see Details. Default 1.

Value

A length one integer giving the pilot sample size.

Details

If the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) were known, the smallest sample size with risk at most w would be \(n^* = (B/w)^{2/k}\sigma^2\), where \(B = A\,2^{k/2}\,\Gamma\{(k+1)/2\}/\sqrt{\pi}\) (see seq_br_norm_mean). The pilot must be chosen before anything is known about \(\sigma\), so it uses only the known constant \((B/w)^{2/k}\): $$m = \max\{m_0,\ \lceil \{(B/w)^{2/k}\}^{1/(1 + \gamma)} \rceil\}.$$ With the default \(\gamma = 1\) the second term is the square root of that constant, which grows more slowly than \(n^*\) as w shrinks. It therefore does not presume a value of \(\sigma\): a pilot equal to \(n^*\) evaluated at \(\sigma = 1\) is far too large when the standard deviation is well below 1 in the units of the data, and far too small to protect against early stopping when it is well above 1.

This is the package's pilot rule, of the same form as the pilot sample sizes of the package's other sequential procedures (Chattopadhyay and Kelley, 2016, Equation 24; Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay, 2018, Equation 21). It should not be read as the pilot size prescribed by Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009).

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

Examples

# Mean absolute error of at most 0.25 points on a satisfaction scale
seq_br_norm_mean_pilot(A = 1, k = 1, w = 0.25)
#> [1] 10
# Mean squared error of at most 0.01
seq_br_norm_mean_pilot(A = 1, k = 2, w = 0.01)
#> [1] 10
